title: Why the Omer mourns (Yevamot 62b)
hook: the Talmud says Akiva's students died in these weeks for not honoring each other

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lag BaOmer, bonfires and Rabbi Shimon. Your line was a break in the sadness. Did you give someone a bright moment? Today, the sadness itself: why these weeks mourn at all. Day six hundred eighty-six.

Twelve thousand pairs of students. That's the number the Talmud gives for the disciples of Rabbi Akiva, spread across the land from Gevat to Antipatris. A whole generation of learners, studying in pairs, arguing over the words of the Torah. If any group seemed set to carry the tradition forward, it was this one. And according to the Talmud, in a single season, all of them died. The Talmud's explanation isn't about war, or a lack of learning. It's about how they treated each other.
screen: `THE GREATEST SCHOOL OF ITS AGE.` → `THOUSANDS OF STUDENTS.` → `GONE IN A FEW WEEKS.`

segments.voice: The passage is in tractate Yevamot, page 62b. Twelve thousand pairs means twenty-four thousand students. And all of them died in one period, because they did not treat each other with respect. The Talmud adds: they died between Passover and Shavuot. And the world, it says, was desolate. Then Akiva went south and taught just five new students. Among them were Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, whom we met yesterday. Those five carried the Torah forward. Now hear the irony. Rabbi Akiva is the one who called the verse from Leviticus, in the old Jewish translation, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," a great principle of the Torah. Set that beside the Talmud's account: his own students fell short of that very teaching. They knew the texts. They didn't honor the people learning beside them. Some historians suggest the deaths may also reflect the Bar Kokhba revolt against Rome, in which Akiva supported the rebels; the Talmud doesn't say so. Either way, the rabbis chose to remember it as a lesson about respect. That's why, in many communities, these weeks carry quiet mourning: no weddings, no haircuts, no live music, for part of the Omer. Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities count the mourning days differently. And some teachers turn the mourning into a task. If the students died for lack of honoring each other, the repair is to honor each other more. Especially, they say, the people you argue with.
screen: `TWELVE THOUSAND PAIRS.` · `NO RESPECT FOR EACH OTHER.` · `FIVE STUDENTS IN THE SOUTH.` · `LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR, AKIVA TAUGHT.` · then, large: `HONOR EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone today. Breathe, and think of someone you work, study or live beside, especially someone you disagree with, or compete with, or take for granted. Picture their face. Now name one thing about them that deserves honor: their effort, their honesty, their patience, a skill you don't have. Hold that thought until it feels true. Then decide how you'll show it today, in words or in a small act. The bell holds the time.
Rabbi Akiva, whose twenty-four thousand students all died in one season, the Talmud says, because they did not treat each other with respect.

Your line: honor each other. A week of enough, as if you left, an open door, a song of songs, one quality, a break in the sadness, and now honor. Today, tell the person you pictured the thing you honor in them. Day six hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: During part of the Omer period, many Jews refrain from weddings, haircuts and live music in mourning for Rabbi Akiva's students; Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities count the mourning days differently, and many lift the customs on Lag BaOmer.

options: go south and teach five new students.
write down everything you know and retire.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): rewrote the hook, which opened with the banned "Picture", called Akiva's school "the greatest" and him "the most famous", and invented details (memorized tractates, "almost all"); it now starts from the Talmud's own number and range (Gevat to Antipatris). The irony line is framed as a reading, and "many teachers" became "some".

Yevamot 62b paraphrased: 12,000 pairs from Gevat to Antipatris; 'shelo nahagu kavod zeh la-zeh'; died between Pesach and Atzeret; five southern students (Meir, Yehudah, Yossi, Shimon, Elazar ben Shammua). Verify the Hebrew in the original game.
Sifra Kedoshim: Akiva's 'zeh klal gadol baTorah'; reference to verify.
